newsitem.title: TANZANIA: High-level corruption dogs Tanzanian-Nordic ties.
newsitem.headline: High-level corruption dogs Tanzanian-Nordic ties.

text.p: High-level corruption in Tanzania is a major problem in the long-standing aid relationship with Nordic countries, the head of Sweden's aid agency has warned.

"We're talking about corruption which has come about by greed which we think has come into their society," said Bo Goransson, director-general of the Swedish International Development Agency, after two-days of meetings with Tanzanian officials on future aid policy.
Goransson said that while no specific cases of corruption were raised during the meeting, the Tanzanian side freely acknowledged the extent of the problem.
Last month Prime Minister Frederick Sumaye reaffirmed the government's will to tackle corruption, specifically bribery, and appealed for the public's help.
Goransson said the Nordic group was waiting for the government's words to be translated into deeds.
"Unless the government does that, uses the judiciary, uses the law, one gradually loses credibility," he told reporters on Friday night.
The group of Sweden, Denmark, Norway and Finland has been Tanzania's biggest aid provider since independence in 1961, with annual levels of aid currently running at about $150 million.
The partnership flourished under close political ties between Scandinavian leaders and the East African country's founding father and first president, Julius Nyerere.
Nyerere's brand of African Socialism built national unity and eschewed corruption but his failed economic policies left Tanzania marooned near the bottom of the world's poverty index.
Corruption spread after Nyerere's retirement in 1985 and mushroomed during moves to liberalisation in the past few years, local and foreign analysts say.
Despite Goransson's admonishments, Sweden on Saturday handed over a $7 million aid package to Tanzania to help pay off state employees made redundant as part of economic reforms.
